claim: The duration of starvation determines whether Drosophila melanogaster forms appetitive short-term or longer-lasting intermediate memories.
source: We show that the duration of starvation determines whether Drosophila melanogaster forms appetitive short-term or longer-lasting intermediate memories.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Internal glycogen storage in muscles and adipose tissue influences how intensely sucrose-associated information is stored.
source: The internal glycogen storage in the muscles and adipose tissue influences how intensely sucrose-associated information is stored.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing manipulation of glycogen levels affects memory performance.

claim: Insulin-like signaling in octopaminergic reward neurons integrates internal energy storage into memory formation.
source: Insulin-like signaling in octopaminergic reward neurons integrates internal energy storage into memory formation.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 7 showing blocking insulin receptor in octopaminergic neurons affects memory.

claim: Octopamine suppresses the formation of long-term memory.
source: Octopamine, in turn, suppresses the formation of long-term memory.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing octopamine feeding blocks memory and octopamine receptor antagonists induce memory.

claim: Octopamine is not required for short-term memory formation.
source: Octopamine is not required for short-term memory because octopamine-deficient mutants can form appetitive short-term memory for sucrose and to other nutrients depending on the internal energy status.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 1 and 6 showing TβhnM18 mutants can form STM under certain conditions.

claim: Octopamine-deficient mutants can form appetitive short-term memory for sucrose depending on internal energy status.
source: Octopamine is not required for short-term memory because octopamine-deficient mutants can form appetitive short-term memory for sucrose and to other nutrients depending on the internal energy status.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 1B, 1C, and 6 showing TβhnM18 mutants form STM after prolonged starvation or with reduced glycogen.

claim: The reduced positive reinforcing effect of sucrose at high internal glycogen levels could lead to increased food intake.
source: The reduced positive reinforcing effect of sucrose at high internal glycogen levels, combined with the increased stability of food-related memories due to prolonged periods of starvation, could lead to increased food intake.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract as a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Increased stability of food-related memories due to prolonged starvation could lead to increased food intake.
source: The reduced positive reinforcing effect of sucrose at high internal glycogen levels, combined with the increased stability of food-related memories due to prolonged periods of starvation, could lead to increased food intake.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract as a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster uses glucose as its primary energy source.
source: Similar to vertebrates, the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster uses glucose as its primary energy source and stores glycogen primarily in the muscles – the main site of energy expenditure – and the fat body – the equivalent of the vertebrate liver (Gáliková and Klepsatel, 2023; Wigglesworth, 1949).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Drosophila stores glycogen primarily in muscles and fat body.
source: Similar to vertebrates, the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster uses glucose as its primary energy source and stores glycogen primarily in the muscles – the main site of energy expenditure – and the fat body – the equivalent of the vertebrate liver (Gáliková and Klepsatel, 2023; Wigglesworth, 1949).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Muscles are the main site of energy expenditure in Drosophila.
source: Similar to vertebrates, the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster uses glucose as its primary energy source and stores glycogen primarily in the muscles – the main site of energy expenditure – and the fat body – the equivalent of the vertebrate liver (Gáliková and Klepsatel, 2023; Wigglesworth, 1949).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The fat body is the equivalent of the vertebrate liver in Drosophila.
source: Similar to vertebrates, the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster uses glucose as its primary energy source and stores glycogen primarily in the muscles – the main site of energy expenditure – and the fat body – the equivalent of the vertebrate liver (Gáliková and Klepsatel, 2023; Wigglesworth, 1949).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Glycogen levels are found in the Drosophila brain.
source: As in vertebrates, glycogen levels are also found in the brain (Yamada et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Octopamine is functionally related to noradrenalin in vertebrates.
source: In Drosophila, the monoamine octopamine – functionally related to noradrenalin in vertebrates – is involved in the regulation of energy homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Octopamine is involved in the regulation of energy homeostasis in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, the monoamine octopamine – functionally related to noradrenalin in vertebrates – is involved in the regulation of energy homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by subsequent citations.

claim: In Tβh mutants lacking octopamine, glucose and trehalose concentrations in the hemolymph change less upon starvation.
source: In tyramine-β-hydroxylase (Tβh) mutants lacking the neurotransmitter octopamine, the glucose and trehalose concentrations in the hemolymph change less upon starvation, and the life span is extended (Damrau et al., 2017; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Tβh mutants have extended life span.
source: In tyramine-β-hydroxylase (Tβh) mutants lacking the neurotransmitter octopamine, the glucose and trehalose concentrations in the hemolymph change less upon starvation, and the life span is extended (Damrau et al., 2017; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Tβh mutants show an increased threshold to respond to sucrose with proboscis extension.
source: Tβh mutants show an increased threshold to respond to sucrose with the extension of their proboscis when sucrose is offered to their tarsi – a structure that contains gustatory receptor neurons.
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by subsequent citations.

claim: The reduced responsiveness to sucrose correlates with reduced sucrose intake in Tβh mutants.
source: The reduced responsiveness to sucrose correlates with a reduced sucrose intake in Tβh mutants (Li et al., 2016; Scheiner et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Octopaminergic neurons potentiate the response of sugar-sensing gustatory receptor neurons in satiated flies.
source: Octopaminergic neurons potentiate the response of sugar-sensing gustatory receptor neurons in satiated flies, suggesting that octopaminergic neurons regulate feeding behavior by changing the sensitivity of taste receptor neurons (Youn et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Tβh mutants fail to form a positive association with a food reward in classical olfactory conditioning directly after learning.
source: Flies quickly learn to associate an odorant with sucrose, and Tβh mutants do not show this positive association directly after learning (Schwaerzel et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Memory appears in Tβh mutants when a longer time after training has elapsed.
source: However, when a longer time after training has elapsed, memory appears (Das et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The release of octopamine mediates the reinforcing effect of sweet taste in short-term memory.
source: The release of octopamine mediates the reinforcing effect of sweet taste in short-term memory (STM) and the anesthesia-resistant form of long-term memory (LTM) (Burke et al., 2012; Huetteroth et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The release of octopamine mediates the reinforcing effect of sweet taste in anesthesia-resistant long-term memory.
source: The release of octopamine mediates the reinforcing effect of sweet taste in short-term memory (STM) and the anesthesia-resistant form of long-term memory (LTM) (Burke et al., 2012; Huetteroth et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Insulin regulates glucose homeostasis at the cellular level.
source: The peptide hormone insulin regulates glycose homeostasis at the cellular level (Saltiel and Kahn, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Insulin-like peptides in Drosophila perform their functions through well-conserved signal transduction cascades.
source: Insulin and its Drosophila counterpart, insulin-like peptides, perform their functions through well-conserved signal transduction cascades (Chatterjee and Perrimon, 2021; Inoue et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The insulin receptor is broadly expressed in the vertebrate brain and regulates neuronal plasticity.
source: In vertebrates, in addition to its function in fat tissue and muscles, the insulin receptor is broadly expressed in the brain and regulates neuronal plasticity (Nakai et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Reduced insulin receptor function in the rat hypothalamus results in loss of long-term potentiation and impaired spatial memory.
source: For example, in rats, reduced insulin receptor function in the hypothalamus results in loss of long-term potentiation and impaired spatial memory (Grillo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The insulin receptor substrate Chico is required for the development of mushroom bodies in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, the insulin receptor substrate Chico is required for the development of mushroom bodies, a brain region required for learning and memory, and loss of Chico results in learning defects (Naganos et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Loss of Chico results in learning defects in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, the insulin receptor substrate Chico is required for the development of mushroom bodies, a brain region required for learning and memory, and loss of Chico results in learning defects (Naganos et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Disrupting the function of the insulin receptor in mushroom bodies results in learning defects.
source: Disrupting the function of the insulin receptor in the mushroom bodies also results in learning defects, whereas the insulin receptor and Chico are required in the ellipsoid body for protein biosynthesis-dependent LTM (Chambers et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The insulin receptor and Chico are required in the ellipsoid body for protein biosynthesis-dependent LTM.
source: Disrupting the function of the insulin receptor in the mushroom bodies also results in learning defects, whereas the insulin receptor and Chico are required in the ellipsoid body for protein biosynthesis-dependent LTM (Chambers et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Starvation increases learning and memory performance when using a food-related reward.
source: Starvation increases learning and memory performance when using a food-related reward (Colomb et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Flies starved for 16 hr established a positive association between the odorant and the reward that was remembered for 2 min but not for 6 hr or 24 hr.
source: Flies that were starved for 16 hr established a positive association between the odorant and the reward. They remembered this association for 2 min, but not for 6 hr or 24 hr.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Learning and memory performance was significantly improved by prolonged starvation from 16 hr to 40 hr.
source: Consistent with previous results, learning and memory performance was significantly improved by prolonged starvation (Colomb et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1B and a citation.

claim: Memory after prolonged starvation was still detectable 6 hr after training.
source: The memory was also remembered for longer since it was still detectable 6 hr after training.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: TβhnM18 mutants starved for 16 hr did not show 2 min memory but showed memory 6 hr later that lasted up to 24 hr.
source: The TβhnM18 mutants starved for 16 hr did not show 2 min memory but emerged memory 6 hr later that lasted up to 24 hr (Das et al., 2014; Schwaerzel et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1B and citations.

claim: TβhnM18 mutants remembered the rewarded odorant after 2 min following starvation extended to 40 hr.
source: In contrast, TβhnM18 mutants remembered the rewarded odorant after only 2 min following starvation extended to 40 hr.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The memory in 40 hr-starved TβhnM18 mutants was still detectable after 6 hr and 24 hr.
source: The memory was still detectable after 6 hr and 24 hr (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 16 hr-starved TβhnM18 mutants form a negative association with 0.15 M sucrose directly after training.
source: In contrast to the experiments using 2 M sucrose as a reward, 16 hr-starved TβhnM18 mutants form a negative association with 0.15 M sucrose directly after the training, which turns into a positive association when the flies were starved longer 40 hr.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The negative association with 0.15 M sucrose in TβhnM18 mutants turns into a positive association after 40 hr starvation.
source: In contrast to the experiments using 2 M sucrose as a reward, 16 hr-starved TβhnM18 mutants form a negative association with 0.15 M sucrose directly after the training, which turns into a positive association when the flies were starved longer 40 hr.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Prolonged starvation significantly increased learning and memory performance in controls and TβhnM18 mutants when using 0.15 M sucrose.
source: Again, prolonged starvation significantly increased learning and memory performance in controls and TβhnM18 mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The length of starvation and the reinforcer strength influence appetitive memory strength.
source: Thus, the length of starvation and the reinforcer strength influence appetitive memory strength.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Protein synthesis-dependent LTM is labile immediately after training and can be blocked by 4°C cold-shock anesthesia.
source: Protein synthesis-dependent LTM is still labile immediately after training and can be blocked by 4°C cold-shock anesthesia immediately after training.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: After consolidation, LTM is cold-shock-resistant and insensitive to a cold shock 1 hr before the test.
source: After consolidation, LTM is cold-shock-resistant and insensitive to a cold shock 1 hr before the test (Krashes and Waddell, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Memory in 16 hr-starved control flies was completely abolished by cold shock directly after training or shortly before the test.
source: The memory was completely abolished by a cold shock directly after training or shortly before the test.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Prolonging starvation resulted in memory that was sensitive to cold shock directly after training but not shortly before the test.
source: Prolonging the starvation period resulted in memory that was sensitive to cold shock directly after training but not shortly before the test.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 16 hr-starved TβhnM18 mutants developed memory that was sensitive to cold shock directly after training and cold-shock-insensitive shortly before the test.
source: In contrast, 16 hr-starved TβhnM18 mutants developed memory that was sensitive to cold shock directly after training and cold-shock-insensitive shortly before the test.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 16 hr-starved TβhnM18 mutants develop LTM.
source: The results, together with the observed memory 24 hr later of TβhnM18 after the same training (Figure 1B), support that TβhnM18 mutant develop LTM.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B and 2A.

claim: Longer periods of starvation in TβhnM18 mutants resulted in anesthesia-resistant LTM.
source: Longer periods of starvation in TβhnM18 mutants resulted in anesthesia-resistant LTM.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Blocking neuronal activity of R15A04-Gal4 targeted neurons immediately after training results in TβhnM18 mutants losing LTM.
source: Blocking the function of these dopaminergic neurons immediately after training using a temperature-sensitive shibire transgene (UAS-shits) and a 30 min heat pulse of 31°C resulted in loss of memory in TβhnM18 mutants (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: R15A04-Gal4 driver targets dopaminergic neurons of the PAM cluster, which are specifically required for appetitive LTM but not STM.
source: The R15A04-Gal4 driver targets dopaminergic neurons of the PAM cluster, which are specifically required for appetitive LTM but not STM (Yamagata et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Lightly hungry flies form a memory that lasts up to 3 hr and is sensitive to anesthesia.
source: These results, together with the course of memory loss, show that lightly hungry flies form a memory that lasts up to 3 hr and is sensitive to anesthesia (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and summarized in Figure 2C.

claim: Since no memory can be observed 24 hr later in 16 hr-starved control flies, this indicates that it is an anesthesia-sensitive intermediate memory (ITM).
source: Since no memory can be observed 24 hr later, this indicates that it is an anesthesia-sensitive intermediate memory (ITM).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Prolonged starvation results in anesthesia-resistant ITM in control flies.
source: Prolonged starvation results in anesthesia-resistant ITM (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and summarized in Figure 2C.

claim: Mildly starved TβhnM18 mutants form a LTM that is sensitive to anesthesia and detectable 24 hr after training.
source: In contrast, mildly starved TβhnM18 mutants form a LTM that is sensitive to anesthesia-sensitive and detectable 24 hr after the training.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B and 2A and summarized in Figure 2C.

claim: Prolonged starvation in TβhnM18 mutants leads to anesthesia-resistant LTM and short-term memory.
source: Prolonged starvation in TβhnM18 mutants leads to anesthesia-resistant LTM (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B and 2A and summarized in Figure 2C.

claim: Feeding the octopamine antagonist epinastine for 1 hr immediately after training resulted in memory 5 hr later in control flies.
source: To do so, we first blocked the function of octopamine receptors in controls immediately after the training by feeding the octopamine antagonist epinastine for 1 hr and analyzed memory 5 hr later (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Feeding octopamine to TβhnM18 mutants immediately after training blocked LTM.
source: Consistent with the idea that octopamine is a negative regulator of LTM, feeding octopamine to TβhnM18 mutants immediately after training blocked LTM (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A short pulse of octopamine before training inhibits STM in control flies.
source: A short pulse of octopamine before the training inhibits STM.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Octopamine is a negative regulator of appetitive LTM and STM.
source: Taken together, octopamine is a negative regulator of appetitive LTM and STM (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Flies fed with octopamine showed a significant reduction of sucrose intake.
source: Flies fed with octopamine showed a significant reduction of sucrose intake, but not flies fed with a similar amount of tyramine or a tenfold increase in tyramine concentration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Flies fed with tyramine did not show a reduction in sucrose intake.
source: Flies fed with octopamine showed a significant reduction of sucrose intake, but not flies fed with a similar amount of tyramine or a tenfold increase in tyramine concentration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Increased octopamine content influences how food is evaluated.
source: Therefore, it is possible that increased octopamine content influences how food is evaluated.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Octopamine functions as a signal for food or high internal energy levels.
source: This is consistent with a function of octopamine as a signal for food or high internal energy levels.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: In controls and TβhnM18 mutants, starvation reduces the glycogen level.
source: In controls and TβhnM18 mutants, starvation reduces the glycogen level.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Non-starved TβhnM18 mutant males had significantly higher glycogen levels at baseline than controls.
source: However, non-starved TβhnM18 mutant males had significantly higher glycogen levels at baseline.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: After 40 hr of starvation, the glycogen levels of TβhnM18 mutants were still higher than those of controls starved for the same amount of time.
source: After 40 hr of starvation, the glycogen levels of TβhnM18 mutants were still higher than those of controls that were starved for the amount of time.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Non-starved flies reared on standard fly food preferred sucrose over protein-enriched food.
source: Non-starved flies reared on standard fly food preferred sucrose over protein-enriched food, but TβhnM18 mutants to a significantly lesser extent than controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: TβhnM18 mutants showed a significantly lower preference for sucrose over protein-enriched food than controls.
source: Non-starved flies reared on standard fly food preferred sucrose over protein-enriched food, but TβhnM18 mutants to a significantly lesser extent than controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 18 hr of starvation resulted in a decreased sucrose preference in controls and TβhnM18 mutants.
source: Also, 18 hr of starvation resulted in a decreased sucrose preference in controls and TβhnM18 mutants, but to a significantly lower level in TβhnM18 mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Extending the starvation period to 40 hr resulted in similar sucrose consumption in control and mutant flies.
source: Extending the starvation period to 40 hr resulted in a similar sucrose consumption in control and mutant flies.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Male flies fed standard food for 3 d strongly preferred sucrose over protein-enriched food, with TβhnM18 mutants showing a significant reduction.
source: Male flies fed standard food for 3 d strongly preferred sucrose over protein-enriched food, with TβhnM18 mutants showing a significant reduction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Yeast-deprived and sucrose-deprived TβhnM18 mutants showed a significantly reduced preference for sucrose.
source: Yeast-deprived and sucrose-deprived TβhnM18 mutant showed a significantly reduced preference for sucrose.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In mated females, no differences were observed in food preference between controls and the TβhnM18 mutant.
source: In mated females, no differences were observed in food preference between controls and the TβhnM18 mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The reduced preference for sucrose consumption correlates in TβhnM18 with increased glycogen levels.
source: In conclusion, the reduced preference for sucrose consumption correlates in TβhnM18 with increased glycogen levels.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: TβhnM18 mutants can sense the reduction of specific internal energy stores and change their food preferences accordingly.
source: Furthermore, TβhnM18 mutants can sense the reduction of specific internal energy stores and change their food preferences accordingly.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Glycogen is mainly found in the fat bodies and the muscles in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, glycogen is mainly found in the fat bodies – the major energy storage organ – and the muscles, a major site of energy expenditure (Wigglesworth, 1949).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Glycogen synthase and glycogen phosphorylase control glycogen content in the body.
source: Glycogen synthase and glycogen phosphorylase control glycogen content in the body (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is stated as established knowledge and illustrated in Figure 5A.

claim: Knockdown of glycogen synthase using GlySHMS01279-RNAi efficiently reduced glycogen levels in larvae.
source: Glycogen synthase and glycogen phosphorylase control glycogen content in the body (Figure 5A). Knockdown of glycogen synthase using GlySHMS01279-RNAi efficiently reduced glycogen levels in larvae, while knockdown of glycogen phosphorylase using GlyPHMS00032-RNAi efficiently increased glycogen levels (Yamada et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Knockdown of glycogen phosphorylase using GlyPHMS00032-RNAi efficiently increased glycogen levels in larvae.
source: Glycogen synthase and glycogen phosphorylase control glycogen content in the body (Figure 5A). Knockdown of glycogen synthase using GlySHMS01279-RNAi efficiently reduced glycogen levels in larvae, while knockdown of glycogen phosphorylase using GlyPHMS00032-RNAi efficiently increased glycogen levels (Yamada et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Increasing glycogen levels in the muscles had no effect on the STM of 16 hr-starved flies.
source: Increasing glycogen levels in the muscles had no effect on the STM of the 16 hr-starved flies, but decreasing glycogen levels significantly improved memory performance (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Decreasing glycogen levels in muscles significantly improved memory performance.
source: Increasing glycogen levels in the muscles had no effect on the STM of the 16 hr-starved flies, but decreasing glycogen levels significantly improved memory performance (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Increasing or decreasing glycogen levels in the fat bodies had no effect on memory performance.
source: Increasing or decreasing glycogen levels in the fat bodies had no effect on memory performance (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: When the muscles and fat bodies glycogen levels were significantly increased, flies showed a reduced memory to odorants paired with sucrose.
source: When the muscles and fat bodies glycogen levels were significantly increased, flies showed a reduced memory to odorants paired with sucrose.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: An increase in memory performance was observed when glycogen levels were significantly reduced in both muscles and fat bodies.
source: An increase in memory performance was observed when glycogen levels were significantly reduced in both tissues (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Energy metabolism in mushroom bodies is important for the formation of LTM.
source: Recently, it has been shown that energy metabolism in mushroom bodies is important for the formation of LTM (Plaçais et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Low levels of glycogen in the muscles after starvation positively influence appetitive STM.
source: Thus, low levels of glycogen in the muscles after starvation positively influence appetitive STM, whereas high levels of glycogen in the muscles and fat body decrease reduce STM.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claim: High levels of glycogen in the muscles and fat body reduce STM.
source: Thus, low levels of glycogen in the muscles after starvation positively influence appetitive STM, whereas high levels of glycogen in the muscles and fat body decrease reduce STM.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Reduction of glycogen in muscles or fat bodies alone in TβhnM18 mutants did not improve STM.
source: Neither the reduction in the muscles nor the reduction in fat bodies of TβhnM18 mutants improved STM.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: When glycogen was reduced in both muscles and fat bodies, TβhnM18 mutants showed improved STM compared to controls.
source: Only when glycogen was reduced in both tissues did the TβhnM18 mutants show improved STM compared to controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: TβhnM18 mutant flies can form appetitive STM similar to controls when the energy storage is sufficiently reduced.
source: Thus, TβhnM18 mutant flies can form appetitive STM similar to controls when the energy storage is sufficiently reduced.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: Non-starved TβhnM18 mutant males have a significantly higher protein intake than controls.
source: Non-starved TβhnM18 mutant males have a significantly higher protein intake than controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: After 16 hr of starvation, the protein intake of TβhnM18 mutants was comparable to that of control flies.
source: However, after 16 hr of starvation, the protein intake was comparable to that of control flies.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Male TβhnM18 mutants showed comparable STM levels to controls when 5% yeast was used as a food reward.
source: When 5% yeast was used as a food reward, male TβhnM18 mutants showed comparable STM levels controls (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Virgin females showed a higher consumption preference for sucrose than mated females when given the choice between yeast and sucrose.
source: Virgin females showed a higher consumption preference for sucrose than mated females when given the choice between yeast and sucrose (Figure 4C), demonstrating a difference in internal energy demands and suggesting a difference in valence for different diets.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Virgin females remembered the odorant paired with sucrose significantly better than mated females.
source: Virgin females showed a higher consumption preference for sucrose than mated females when given the choice between yeast and sucrose (Figure 4C), demonstrating a difference in internal energy demands and suggesting a difference in valence for different diets. We tested virgin and mated female flies of controls and TβhnM18 mutants for STM with 2 M sucrose as reinforcer (Figure 6C). Virgin females remembered the odorant paired with sucrose significantly better than mated females.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Virgin TβhnM18 mutant females remembered the odorant paired with sucrose significantly better than mated TβhnM18 mutant females.
source: This was also true for TβhnM18 mutant females.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The internal energy status influences how the reward is evaluated in learning and memory.
source: Thus, the internal energy status influences how the reward is evaluated in learning and memory.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: Insulin-like signaling regulates glycogen levels in invertebrates and vertebrates.
source: Insulin-like signaling regulates glycogen levels in invertebrates and vertebrates (Semaniuk et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Loss of the insulin receptor results in more circulating sugar but not increased glycogen levels.
source: Loss of the insulin receptor results in more circulating sugar but not increased glycogen levels (Shingleton et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Activated InR is broadly expressed in a punctate manner throughout the brain and more specifically in the soma of dTdc2-Gal4-targeted neurons.
source: In the brain, activated InR is broadly expressed in a punctate manner and more specifically in the soma of dTdc2-Gal4-targeted neurons (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The expression of activated InR using UAS-InR.A1325D under the control of the dTdc2-Gal4 driver resulted in increased immunoreactivity.
